items.name: Amazon
items.description: Amazon's bar leans on Leadership Principles and scenario thinking more than raw algorithm difficulty. Coding rounds skew toward OOD and under-specified prompts that reward clarification skill, and a GenAI-usage behavioral question appears in nearly every modern loop. Bar Raiser independence and writing-heavy work samples shape the senior-level signal.

items.name: Apple
items.description: Apple interviews are unusually team-owned: the same company can run classic LeetCode screens, MLE case studies, hardware verification drills, project deep-dives, and system design loops with little advance disclosure. The strongest pattern is role fit: interviewers probe whether your prior work maps directly to the team's product surface, data domain, and engineering stack, while still expecting clean code, concise trade-off reasoning, and polished behavioral stories.

items.name: Google
items.description: Google's loop runs on hiring-committee arbitration, with a separate team-match phase deciding whether HC approval turns into an offer. Coding bars are remarkably consistent across teams; leveling rigor and behavioral depth drive most of the L3–L6 differentiation.

items.name: Uber
items.description: Uber's loop leans heavily on Uber Eats and rider/driver marketplace problems — Cart pricing, geo heatmaps, surge, and restaurant recommendation surface in nearly every onsite at L5+. Coding rounds are mostly tagged LeetCode patterns, but Hack2Hire OAs ship a small rotating set of original problems that rarely appear elsewhere. Coding bar is the gate; system design quality drives leveling between L5a / L5b / Senior / Staff.

items.name: Bytedance
items.description: ByteDance / TikTok runs a strict one-round-at-a-time funnel with sharp org-by-org variance in bar, language, and round mix. Coding rounds skew toward classic LeetCode-medium with one self-built test case; MLE and SRE loops front-load 30+ minutes of oral 八股 before any code is written. Interviewer professionalism varies — strong candidates drive the round structurally rather than waiting to be assessed.

items.name: Snowflake
items.description: Snowflake's loop is small and bank-driven: a recruiter screen, two back-to-back coding phone screens, then a virtual onsite that mixes coding, system design, and behavioral. The same handful of coding families (multi-source BFS on a grid, course-schedule variants, tree-node-deletion height problems, transactional KV stores) cycle through most candidates, so recognition speed matters more than novel problem solving.

items.name: Microsoft
items.description: Microsoft runs two parallel hiring tracks: the standardized Hiring Event (HE) loop covering Azure, Cloud, Copilot, and Office orgs, and Mustafa Suleyman's MAI org with its own recruiter pool and a distinctly OpenAI-flavored coding rotation. The HE bar is consistent — four 60-minute rounds back-to-back on a fixed weekday — with medium-difficulty algorithms and one system-design slot; MAI loops add project deep-dive depth and pull problems from an in-memory-DB / beam-search / streaming-decoder pool that does not overlap with classic LeetCode prep.

items.name: Karat
items.description: Karat conducts outsourced technical screens on behalf of hiring companies, so the round follows Karat's format rather than the hiring team's. Rounds are tightly time-boxed and multi-part, and reading speed on a long prompt or unfamiliar starter code matters about as much as coding speed.

items.name: Openai
items.description: OpenAI pairs an unusually high raw-coding bar with explicit no-AI-tools rules during most interviews — a deliberate contrast with the product. Phone screens often run a single multi-part simulation for the full hour, and senior loops add deep ML and research-grounded system-design rounds that probe mechanism, not vocabulary.

items.name: Meta
items.description: Meta sits mid-transition between two interview loops in 2026. The legacy track still drives most candidates through CodeSignal-style OAs and tightly time-boxed coding rounds, while a new AI-Native loop layers in AI-assisted coding, AI-Enabled system design, and an AI-oriented behavioral round on top. Which track you land in depends on org and recruiter, not candidate preference.

items.name: Oracle
items.description: Oracle's loops split along two clear axes: OCI (Cloud Infrastructure) runs a fairly standard LC + system-design loop with heavy Indian interviewer rotation, while OHAI (Oracle Health, the post-Cerner business unit) leans into OOD/class-design problems built around healthcare scenarios. Coding bars are mostly easy-to-medium, but interviewer variance and post-loop down-leveling / ghosting are unusually common — the loop result often determines the eventual level, not just the yes/no.

items.name: Capital One
items.description: Capital One's engineering loop is unusually predictable: a long CodeSignal OA gates everyone, then a single Power Day stitches four 45-60 minute rounds — coding, system design, case study, and behavioral — back to back. The technical bar is moderate but the case study and BQ rounds carry real weight, especially for MLE / Applied Research / Data Science where the business-context framing of a model decision is the differentiating signal.

items.name: Stripe
items.description: Stripe favors long realistic prompts in a full IDE — integration, debugging, refactor — over LeetCode-style algorithms. System design is grounded in payments and regulatory reality, and behavioral signals weigh ownership and written communication as heavily as raw technical depth.

items.name: C3.ai
items.description: C3 AI runs a compact, hiring-manager-led loop: a short behavioral conversation with the manager comes first, followed by a two-round onsite of coding and system design where design interviewers push hard on deep dives. New-grad Forward Deployed Engineer candidates start with a HackerRank assessment that blends CS fundamentals, applied-AI judgment, and practical coding.

items.name: Square
items.description: Block (Square, Cash App) screens with practical, multi-part CoderPad problems modeled on real product logic, where tests and clean refactoring between parts matter as much as the algorithm. Senior loops add a conversational round on AI-native engineering workflow, and money-movement teams probe correctness, legacy tech debt, and regulated-system judgment.

items.name: Waymo
items.description: Waymo loops mix nominally LeetCode-style coding with deliberately ambiguous, autonomy-flavored prompts and a signature 'data fluency' round that's hard to drill for. Coding bars are mid-hard but interviewers frequently swap in original problems framed around self-driving scenarios; ML and senior loops add a behavior-prediction-style ML system design round on top.

items.name: LinkedIn
items.description: LinkedIn's loop pivoted heavily in 2025 — Staff candidates now sit a packed two-round phone screen (coding + project retro) before a five-round onsite that includes an AI-Coding session in CoderPad's assistant pane. Behavioural depth is the dominant downlevel axis; the same coding bar that passes at Senior frequently caps a Staff loop with a downlevel offer.

items.name: Airbnb
items.description: Airbnb's loop is famously consistent and famously slow. The coding pool is small and reused — a candidate who has drilled the canonical questions (split-stay, terrain water-drop, KV store, code review) walks in advantaged. Differentiation happens in the code-review round, the experience deep-dive, and the standalone core-values round, which is calibrated separately from the rest of the loop and serves as a real gate. Expect strong technical performance to land in a multi-week team-match queue rather than a fast offer.

items.name: Roblox
items.description: Roblox interviews lean heavily on a small, stable repertoire of coding and system design prompts drawn from the company's own product surface — rate limiting, like-button counters, matchmaking queues, delayed payments. The bar is high but predictable: interviewers want bug-free implementations with crisp boundary handling and design discussions that ground every trade-off in real platform scale (millions of concurrent players, hot creator experiences, cross-region latency). HM and director rounds heavily probe past experience with comparable traffic and scope.

items.name: Pinterest
items.description: Pinterest's loop leans hard on a recurring custom prompt library — escape-room state-tracking, trie-backed access control, ads/log aggregation, splitwise-style settlement — over canonical LeetCode. ML system design is split into two distinct rounds ("ML Practitioner" and "ML System Design") that effectively cover the same recommender / retrieval / ranking surface from two angles, with embedding-heavy product framing throughout. Fully-remote, front-loaded compensation, and long team-match windows define the experience as much as the technical bar.

items.name: Disney
items.description: Disney hires through individual organizations such as Streaming and Experiences, and each hiring manager shapes the loop, so formats vary widely even for the same title. Coding is mostly practical and moderate in difficulty; project depth, collaboration, and trade-off-heavy design discussions carry most of the weight.

items.name: Netflix
items.description: Netflix's current engineering loop is high-signal and repeat-heavy: Ads candidates see the same topo / frequency-cap / ads data-modeling trio, Member-Commerce-Games candidates see homepage dedupe and duplicate-detection variants, and Infra / Data Platform candidates see cache, latency, and concurrency rounds. The technical prompts are usually solvable, but the grading is communication-heavy: candidates are expected to clarify vague requirements, write tests, explain trade-offs, and connect their past work tightly to the target org.

items.name: Citadel
items.description: Citadel and Citadel Securities run two distinct loops sharing one brand. Citsec (the market maker) hires for HFT software, quant research and quant dev; its phone screens lean on small, sharp coding prompts (merge-K, ring buffers, stock-DP ladders) and the loop is famously single-fail — any weak round and the next interview is cancelled within a day. Citadel (the hedge fund) and its sub-orgs (GQS, EQR, NXT) lean harder on probability brainteasers, deep resume drilling and a multi-week team-match stage where coding bar drops but cultural and PM-style fit dominates the offer decision.

items.name: Goldman Sachs
items.description: Goldman Sachs interview loops lean heavily on traditional LeetCode-style coding — the firm publishes its own tagged problem list on LeetCode, and the OA / phone screens recycle from a stable bank that maps closely to it. Behavioral signal is concentrated in a Hirevue video screen with tight 30-second prep windows, and quant-flavored desks (GSAM, Quant Engineering) layer probability and statistics drills on top of the standard coding bar.

items.name: Salesforce
items.description: Salesforce's loop is bank-driven: a small set of coding prompts (LFU Cache, Flatten JSON, linked-list dedup, frontend curry + traffic light, OA HackerRank classics) and one signature system design (Coffee Ordering, with its SQL follow-ups) cover the bulk of recent rounds. Down-leveling at offer time is common — the HM screen and behavioural depth materially shape the final level, often more than coding correctness alone.

items.name: Bloomberg
items.description: Bloomberg's loop is a coding-heavy gauntlet: three back-to-back technical rounds each pack two LeetCode-style problems with little hand-holding, plus an HR screen and an engineering manager round that anchors on a single deep project story. The coding bar emphasizes pristine communication — dry-running, edge cases, and complexity discussion are graded as heavily as the solution itself, and interviewers routinely push for second-best alternatives even after a working answer. New-grad and tech-screen verdicts often arrive within hours, while jump-shift onsites favor candidates who can explain past trade-offs without prompting.

items.name: NURO
items.description: Nuro builds autonomous driving technology and hires engineers who are as comfortable with threads and locks as with algorithms: its coding interviews deliberately split into a classic algorithm track and an OS-and-concurrency systems track. System design leans toward the realities of an autonomous fleet — heavy batch compute and enormous volumes of vehicle data — and the process extends past the onsite into meetings with senior leadership.

items.name: DoorDash
items.description: DoorDash's loop is dominated by a small, slow-moving library of original Code Craft prompts (Dasher Pay, Bootstrap API, Round Robin debugging) plus a handful of recurring system-design favorites (3-day Donation, Notification, Food Review). Coding bar is the gate; system design correctness and behavioral consistency drive leveling. The bar swings sharply with the interviewer — multiple candidates report bug-free coding rounds that still ended in rejection — so prepping the canonical question set cold matters more than chasing breadth.

items.name: Anthropic
items.description: Anthropic runs an unusually small, transparent technical question bank — the recruiter typically names which prompt family you'll see days before the round, so candidates can target preparation precisely instead of guessing. Bars are calibrated for problem-solving velocity and follow-up depth rather than novelty; offers are decided by hiring committee + reference check, and the culture round on AI-safety alignment is the single most common rejection point even for candidates who clear every technical stage.

items.name: Jump Trading
items.description: Jump Trading interviews engineers as low-latency systems builders: after a Codility screen, technical rounds favour hand-built infrastructure — interpreters, concurrent data structures, allocators — over puzzle-style algorithms. Quant research interviews are open-ended, centred on data reasoning and an unusually deep interrogation of past research.

items.name: Databricks
items.description: Databricks interviews are unusually bank-driven: candidates who know the recurring prompt families often recognize the round within the first few minutes. The loop mixes algorithmic coding with low-level systems and product-grounded design, then puts real weight on behavioral, hiring-committee, and reference signals after the technical rounds.

items.name: Jane Street
items.description: Jane Street hires through practical, conversational interviews rather than puzzle-bank recall. Engineering rounds are small, realistic programming tasks written without running code and judged on clarity and correctness, while trading and research loops rely on interactive games, live market making and probability reasoning under persistent questioning.

items.name: Anduril Industries
items.description: Anduril is a defense technology company, and much of its engineering work can only be done on-site, so roles are expected to be in the office. Interviews favor practical, quickly-solvable coding problems over puzzle-heavy ones, and the final round is often a hiring-manager conversation that rewards matching the scope the interviewer has in mind.

items.name: Dropbox
items.description: Dropbox's loop favors practical engineering over puzzle-solving: coding rounds start small and push toward scale and system concerns, and design interviewers probe implementation-level trade-offs. Ownership is tested hard, with a dedicated deep dive into a project you drove.

items.name: Pure Storage
items.description: Pure Storage (now also hiring under the Everpure name) reuses a small, well-known set of coding questions, so loops are decided by depth rather than novelty: interviewers press hard on concurrency, lock discipline and read/write optimization. Experienced loops close with a hiring-manager conversation and an architect-led design round built around real storage problems.

items.name: Snapchat
items.description: Snap interviews are highly interviewer-dependent: candidates report classic graph and cache problems, open-ended backend coding, product-heavy system design, and MLE loops that dig into recommendation systems, ranking, fundamentals, and project judgment. The safest preparation strategy is to be fluent in BFS/DFS, cache/data-structure implementation, feed and ads design, and concise behavioral stories around innovation, ambiguity, and execution.

items.name: Point72 Asset Management
items.description: Point72 hires across discretionary, systematic (Cubist) and data-heavy teams, and each role family runs its own loop. Engineering roles reward practical HackerRank fluency and broad, gap-free fundamentals; research roles test probability, statistics and portfolio-construction intuition alongside a close look at your own strategy work.

items.name: Whatnot
items.description: Whatnot is a live-stream shopping marketplace, and its engineering loop reflects that: engineers are expected to think like users of the app, with product sense assessed alongside coding and system design. Coding screens favor short, practical problems where finishing and testing the follow-ups matters more than algorithmic depth.

items.name: Optiver
items.description: Optiver is a market-making trading firm whose interview process is built to find fast, calibrated decision-makers under pressure. The funnel is dominated by a heavy online assessment — a probability/sequence/reaction battery for quant roles and OOP simulation coding for engineers — and the quant loop centers on a live EV betting game where speed and bet-sizing matter more than ending profit.

items.name: JPMorgan Chase
items.description: JPMorgan Chase's engineering loop is predictable but operationally uneven: a light HackerRank-style OA is followed by a Super Day with coding, code review, system design, and behavioral rounds rotating across candidates. The technical bar skews practical: simple algorithms, review of production-ish Java code, concurrency/style critiques, and system designs around traffic, search, inventory, payments, and URL routing.

items.name: Reddit
items.description: Reddit's loop runs on a small, slowly-rotating bank of company-specific coding prompts (Tennis Scoring, Report Chain, Chat Message Merge) paired with product-flavored system-design rounds (Game Leaderboard, Live Chat, Notification System). The bar is high on clean OOD and crisp clarification — multi-part prompts are routinely under-scoped on purpose, and rounds end without finishing all parts. Ads and ML Platform orgs add a hiring-manager domain round on top of the standard loop; recent cohorts also report aggressive down-leveling and long team-match limbo after a passing loop.

items.name: Adobe
items.description: Adobe has no single company-wide loop: each hiring team defines its own rounds, so a 'coding' interview can turn into system design and an ML screen can mean implementing an algorithm from scratch. Staff loops lean heavily on system design and operational maturity, while MLE loops range from traditional ML to LLM serving and GPU performance.

items.name: NVIDIA
items.description: NVIDIA interviews are highly team-specific and much less LeetCode-bank-driven than most large tech loops. System Software, Linux, Tegra, DGX AI infra, and Deep Learning roles lean toward engineering scenarios: C/C++ debugging, graph validation, GPU / inference fundamentals, small utility coding, and project deep dives; some design and product-facing AI roles add system-design or technical-marketing discussions.

items.name: Coinbase
items.description: Coinbase runs a long, gated pipeline — AI recruiter screen, a cognitive aptitude test, a culture/personality questionnaire, and a CodeSignal coding OA all precede the recruiter call, and team match still happens before the 4-round VO. Coding rounds bias toward multi-level CodeSignal-style problems (banking system, in-memory database, mining-block knapsack, crypto order management) over canonical LeetCode; bring your own scaffolding because interviewers often hand you a blank file with no class structure or tests. AI-assisted coding is now an explicit round on its own.

items.name: Tradedesk
items.description: The Trade Desk's interviews favor practical, simulation-style engineering over puzzle solving, from a levels-based CodeSignal assessment to live rounds drawn from a fixed internal question bank. System design is grounded in its ad-bidding business, where serving read-heavy data at extremely low latency across regions is the central concern.

items.name: Nextdoor
items.description: Nextdoor is a neighborhood-based social network, and its interviews stay close to that product: feeds, posts, comments, and the metrics behind them. The process opens with an unusually heavy two-round phone screen, and decisions are terse and opaque, so polish and speed count even on familiar problems.

items.name: Tesla
items.description: Tesla interviews are highly team-specific: Autopilot, Optimus, Dojo, data engineering, infotainment, and factory-software teams each run their own practical technical screens. The common pattern is a fast transition from resume/project discussion into runnable code, with interviewers pushing for optimality, clean implementation style, and concrete ownership of past technical decisions.

items.name: Confluent
items.description: Confluent runs a compact loop built on a small, recurring pool of practical, systems-flavored coding problems and product-style system design, where API and data-model clarity count for more than diagrams. Since joining IBM, hiring runs through IBM's channels and can include an extra values-alignment step.
